title: I gave Claude Code one night to build a 3D horror arcade in Godot. It worked by 6:31 am and looked like an empty sports hall. Before/after of the notes that fixed it
author: Plastic-Gear-4258
selftext:
I'm not a programmer. At 1:26 am I handed Claude Code a whole game: a haunted 1980s arcade where you insert a soul into a cabinet and the game bursts out into the room.

What the overnight run did on its own:

\- a lead agent plus 7 sub-agents (sound, 3D models, art, three arcade games, the boss) and 2 testing agents

\- 39 props built through code in Blender: pinball machines, a claw machine, a skee-ball lane, a DJ booth, a mirror ball

\- by 6:31 am: an explorable arcade, three playable games, a final boss, and tests where it played the game itself

It all worked. It also looked like an empty sports hall: the floor was a polished mirror, the puddles looked like engine oil, and one game drowned the room in green fog.

What fixed it: notes, not code (paintovers on screenshots helped most):

\- light only from real sources (lamps, screens, candles, neon) plus haze, so you get beams and real darkness between them

\- soft blurred reflections on the wood; only the puddles act as mirrors

\- 3D cobweb strands instead of stickers, and over 3,600 small details placed by code: grouped around the light, piled in corners, walkways left clear

\- a flicker I couldn't name: a test agent filmed the hall at 60 fps with a still camera, measured the brightness frame by frame, and found signs pulsing several times a second plus a setting that made thousands of pixels shimmer

\- one agent played the games 1,016 times and found you could kill the giant skull centipede in 13 seconds, so it rebalanced the fight

The lesson I keep coming back to: AI gives you everything you asked for, not necessarily what you imagined. Describing what the player should feel worked far better than describing the code.

Stack: Claude Code, Godot 4.7, ChatGPT for images, Suno for the music. The game is free (Windows) and there's a 25-minute making-of; links in the first comment. Happy to answer anything about the workflow.

comments.author: Plastic-Gear-4258
comments.body:
Links:

\- Free game (Windows): [https://hallucivids.itch.io/insert-soul](https://hallucivids.itch.io/insert-soul)

\- Full making-of (25 min: the overnight build, every before/after, the flicker hunt, the 13-second boss): [https://youtu.be/v5BILdULltM](https://youtu.be/v5BILdULltM)

If you play it and break something, tell me. After 1,016 bot runs I want to know what the AI missed.

replies.author: Plastic-Gear-4258
replies.body: Ha, thanks! 😄 Imagination was the easy part. Getting the AI to actually match it took a very long list of notes.

comments.author: flockbaygames
comments.body: Going from a mirror floor to light only from real sources is the right call, and with that many lamps I'd bake the ones that never move into a `LightmapGI` and keep real-time shadows on the few that flicker, since every shadowed `OmniLight3D` competes for a slot in the shadow atlas. We build [Flockbay](https://flockbay.com/how-to-make-games-in-claude-code/) for this kind of Claude Code run in Godot, it hosts the Godot editor on Windows and lets Claude Code play the game and take viewport captures over MCP.

replies.author: Plastic-Gear-4258
replies.body: Thanks, good tip! In the hall only 6 of the \~65 lights cast real-time shadows, the rest are unshadowed fills and the bounce light comes from SDFGI. Baking the static ones into LightmapGI is a great next step though, it would free up budget for more volumetric fog. For now Claude plays the game through a scripted bot and captures with Godot's Movie Maker, which works surprisingly well.

comments.author: thundergenie
comments.body: The agent that played 1,016 times just to catch the giant skull centipede dying in 13 seconds deserves a raise.

replies.author: Plastic-Gear-4258
replies.body: I offered it a raise, but it asked for therapy instead 😂
